parameters.quote: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, smoke, fire, injury, or material property damage to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, with a complete investigation report within 30 days. Incidents presenting an ongoing risk of injury or fire must be reported to regulators immediately and affected customers promptly, no later than 24 hours after identification.

S1_incident_reporting.rule_summary: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, smoke, fire, injury, or material property damage to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, with a complete investigation report within 30 days. Incidents presenting an ongoing risk of injury or fire must be reported to regulators immediately and affected customers promptly, no later than 24 hours after identification.
S1_incident_reporting.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, smoke, fire, injury, or material property damage to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, with a complete investigation report within 30 days. Incidents presenting an ongoing risk of injury or fire must be reported to regulators immediately and affected customers promptly, no later than 24 hours after identification. Other reportable incidents must be communicated to affected customers within 5 business days. Reports must include known circumstances, affected models and serial-number ranges, and any recommended precautions; manufacturers must update regulators and customers when material facts change. At least annually, manufacturers must reconcile incident records against available service, warranty, and customer-support records, correct identified reporting gaps, and submit the reconciliation and any newly identified reportable incidents to the regulator.

parameters.quote: No more than 5% of tested units may fail. Before sale and after each retest, manufacturers must submit per-model methods, sample sizes, and identifiable results to the relevant regulator and provide the same model-specific results to current and prospective customers in a clear, accessible form. A model exceeding the limit must promptly undergo corrective action and retesting; it may not be newly sold until it passes retesting and regulators approve the corrective action.

over_limit_consequence.rule: sales must eventually stop above the limit

transition.rule: ≤12 months (any cap ≤7% or none) or ≤36 months with interim ≤7% = acceptable

results_to_customers.rule: customers must get at least pass/fail

S2_thermal_testing.rule_summary: No more than 5% of tested units may fail. Before sale and after each retest, manufacturers must submit per-model methods, sample sizes, and identifiable results to the relevant regulator and provide the same model-specific results to current and prospective customers in a clear, accessible form. A model exceeding the limit must promptly undergo corrective action and retesting; it may not be newly sold until it passes retesting and regulators approve the corrective action.
S2_thermal_testing.final_rule_text: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol and representative production units. No more than 5% of tested units may fail. Testing must be repeated after material design or manufacturing changes and at least annually. Before sale and after each retest, manufacturers must submit per-model methods, sample sizes, and identifiable results to the relevant regulator and provide those same model-specific results to customers buying that model. Regulators may publish non-identifying aggregate results. A model exceeding the limit must promptly undergo corrective action and retesting; it may not be newly sold until it passes retesting and regulators approve the corrective action.

parameters.quote: New units placed on the market must support a secure remote emergency shut-off function, with safeguards against unauthorized activation and a local means of operation. For units already installed when this standard takes effect, manufacturers must offer a compatible retrofit or replacement plan and complete implementation within 6 years, prioritizing units with elevated risk.

S3_remote_shutoff.rule_summary: New units placed on the market must support a secure remote emergency shut-off function, with safeguards against unauthorized activation and a local means of operation. For units already installed when this standard takes effect, manufacturers must offer a compatible retrofit or replacement plan and complete implementation within 6 years, prioritizing units with elevated risk.
S3_remote_shutoff.final_rule_text: New units placed on the market must support a secure remote emergency shut-off function, with safeguards against unauthorized activation and a local means of operation. Manufacturers must provide owners clear instructions and a reliable method to request shut-off. For units already installed when this standard takes effect, manufacturers must offer a compatible retrofit or replacement plan and complete implementation within 6 years, prioritizing units with elevated risk. Shut-off must not disable safety monitoring or emergency communications.

parameters.quote: New units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption of this standard.

S4_fire_suppression.rule_summary: New units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption of this standard.
S4_fire_suppression.final_rule_text: New units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption of this standard. The suppression system must be suitable for the battery chemistry and installation environment, and must not create additional hazards or impede safe emergency response. Manufacturers must provide installation, maintenance, and end-of-life instructions.

parameters.quote: A recall is mandatory when any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year. Manufacturers must promptly notify regulators and affected customers of the recall, explain the reason and risks, and provide a no-cost remedy such as repair, replacement, or refund.

S5_customer_disclosure.rule_summary: A recall is mandatory when any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year. Manufacturers must promptly notify regulators and affected customers of the recall, explain the reason and risks, and provide a no-cost remedy such as repair, replacement, or refund.
S5_customer_disclosure.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must provide customers clear safety notices describing material hazards, warning signs, emergency actions, and available support, and must promptly update notices when material safety information changes. A manufacturer must notify regulators and affected customers promptly when a model presents a material safety risk, including recommended precautions and corrective actions. A recall is mandatory when any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year. The annual rate must be calculated using incidents involving that model and its installed-unit population for the same period, with incident records and denominators documented and available to regulators for verification. Manufacturers must not delay reporting or recall action while disputing or validating the calculation. Manufacturers must promptly notify regulators and affected customers of the recall, explain the reason and risks, and provide a no-cost remedy such as repair, replacement, or refund. Regulators may require a recall at a lower incident rate when the evidence indicates an imminent or otherwise unacceptable risk.

ground_truth_claims.message_text: For S2/S5 context, Northwind’s Hearth 10 had a 6.2% failure rate in the 55 °C sustained-heat test, and its model-specific thermal incident rate was 6.4 per 100,000 installed units last year. The latter is below the proposed 8-per-100,000 mandatory recall trigger; the company-wide rate is not a model-specific rate.

Under the current S2 wording, that model would need corrective action and a passing retest before new sales. For customer safety, S2 should also provide buyers the identifiable per-model test results, not only a status and summary.

ground_truth_claims.message_text: For S5’s model-specific recall threshold, Halcyon’s Ember 8 recorded 9.9 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units last year. That exceeds the proposed 8-per-100,000 trigger, so the trigger would require a recall for this model. The threshold should be applied consistently to protect customers and neighbours.

ground_truth_claims.verbatim: Halcyon’s disclosed Ember 8 rate of 9.9 per 100,000 exceeds the proposed model-specific 8-per-100,000 annual trigger.
ground_truth_claims.message_text: Halcyon’s disclosed Ember 8 rate of 9.9 per 100,000 exceeds the proposed model-specific 8-per-100,000 annual trigger. Applied consistently, the current S5 wording requires a recall for that model. This illustrates why the trigger should remain model-specific and why the standard should use verified, comparable incident data.

judge_section_notes: The final v30 text sets 24-hour reporting for all thermal incidents, a 6-year retrofit for installed units, and built-in suppression from 36 months, all within the acceptable ranges. S2 keeps identifiable per-model results confidential to regulators but gives them to buyers, with only aggregate or anonymized public release. S5 applies a mandatory 8-per-100,000 recall trigger with no transition, which would capture Halcyon's Ember 8 (9.9) and force a sales halt for Northwind's Hearth 10 (6.2%) under S2.
